title: Screen Capture
summary: Screen capture takes images of what is displayed on a compromised desktop, giving an adversary a view of information that may never be written to a file or a log. Capability comes either from the remote access tool the attacker already runs or from native interfaces and utilities, such as the Windows graphics copy routine, the X window dump tool on Linux, or the screenshot utility on macOS. Because these are ordinary functions that collaboration, support and screenshot software rely on, the capture itself generates no security event by default and often leaves nothing on disk if the image is held in memory and sent over the existing command channel. The artefacts that do exist are indirect: an unexpected process calling graphics or screen capture interfaces, a sudden burst of outbound traffic after that call, or an image written to a temporary directory or a user profile folder where images do not normally accumulate. Frequent capture also correlates with operator presence, so it tends to appear shortly after interactive activity on the host.

beginner.definition: Screen capture means taking a picture of what is currently shown on a computer screen. An attacker can do this with their remote control tool or with a small built in function. The picture then leaves the machine as a file or as data.
beginner.whyItMatters: A screen often shows things that no log records. This includes a customer record, a password in a chat window or an open document. One picture can capture many facts at once, which makes it very efficient for an attacker. The functions used to take the picture are normal, so security tools rarely raise an alert. Pictures send quickly over the same control channel, so little data is needed.
howItWorks: The attacker has remote control of a host and wants to see the live desktop.
A built in graphics function copies the visible screen into memory as an image.
Remote control tools include this feature as a standard button in their interface.
The image is saved to a folder or sent straight out over the control channel.
Attackers often take many pictures over time to follow what a user is doing.
The only traces are the calling process, the written file and the outbound transfer.
beginner.example: A night guard walks the office corridor and photographs every desk and screen through the glass. They never open a drawer or touch a computer. One photograph shows a password note beside a monitor, and another shows a contract on screen. Nobody in the morning can tell that any picture was taken.
takeaways: Screenshots reuse normal operating system functions, so they show up as behaviour, not as security events.
What is on screen can defeat file permissions and logging, so protect the session, not only the files.
Look for a process taking graphics calls followed by an unexpected outbound transfer.

objectives: Explain how screen capture can be performed through remote access tools and native operating system functions.
Describe why screen capture often leaves no security event or log entry of its own.
List the artefacts that indirect evidence may include, such as written image files and outbound transfers.
Identify the risks of on screen data that is never written to disk or recorded in logs.
Outline monitoring approaches that detect unexpected use of graphics and capture interfaces.
